reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it favorably presents StrongBlock nodes as a way to earn recurring passive income, highlighting more than €1,350 per month and substantial projected returns while tying participation to buying 10 Strong tokens for about $6,780. The StrongBlock page invites viewers to create a node, and the speaker directs viewers to a description link while acknowledging investment and gas fees and including a disclaimer. The link destination and any actual earnings or losses are not established.

it takes 10 Strong Token to complete a node. Currently it costs 6780 USD

Of course, an investement is really needed
this video is more for people who earn a little more money minimum 6800 dollars

opening.argument: The presentation repeatedly qualifies the opportunity instead of certifying a guaranteed return. It says the token fluctuates, identifies Ethereum gas fees as a cost, acknowledges that the required capital is a “huge investment,” and leaves the decision to each viewer. It also expressly says, “no financial support here in any form.” Those are material risk disclosures: the viewer is told that the asset price changes, withdrawals incur costs, participation requires substantial capital, and the speaker is not providing financial advice. The discussion of projected earnings should therefore be understood as conditional commentary about a volatile crypto project, not a promise that viewers will profit.

citations.quote: What you need to remember is that the coin fluctuates of course
If we have 10, of course that is a huge investment
The question is, should I do that? This is of course left to everyone
Of course, no financial support here in any form

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening emphasizes favorable figures but underweights the warnings accompanying them. The speaker does not hide the purchase requirement or transaction costs; he explicitly says an investment is needed and describes the video as aimed at people with at least $6,800. The figures are presented alongside volatility and gas-fee cautions, so they do not establish a guaranteed outcome or deceptive solicitation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Warnings do not neutralize the central sales impression. The video still calls the project “the most promising option” and presents precise daily, monthly, and yearly earnings. Saying the token fluctuates or that an investment is needed acknowledges risk, but it does not substantiate those projected returns or explain whether the underlying mechanism can sustain them.

opening.argument: This is best read as an explanatory walkthrough of how the StrongBlock concept is supposed to operate. The speaker defines what nodes do, explains that the service handles the node, visits the website, and discusses a calculator-style example. He even says the detailed market guide will not be performed in the video, which indicates commentary and demonstration rather than a completed transaction or proof of earnings. The supplied frames likewise show a node interface, leadership page, and investment calculator, consistent with explaining a product’s claimed operation. Describing a model’s advertised returns is not the same as proving or guaranteeing them.

We will never do that in this video

rebuttal.rebuttal: The educational framing does not erase the subject’s promotional thrust. The speaker repeatedly describes earning regular income, calls the project powerful, and directs viewers to the description link. A calculator demonstration can still function as an inducement when it supplies concrete return projections, even if no completed purchase is shown.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it an explanation does not change what the explanation communicates. The walkthrough links the node directly to recurring earnings, gives the cost of entry, and calculates daily through yearly returns. The interface proves only that a calculator and node page exist; it does not validate the promised economics or make the presentation neutral.

opening.argument: The material describes access to a crypto service and its operating costs, not the hallmark of a conventional scam pitch. The viewer is told that a node requires tokens, that the service runs on Ethereum, and that gas fees apply when rewards are removed. The supplied content does not show a request for passwords, private keys, identity documents, or recruitment of a downline, and it does not state that returns are guaranteed. The website view presents ordinary product controls such as “Create your Node,” while the leadership page identifies named roles. That supports treating this as promotion or commentary about an external service, without certifying that the service is safe.

citations.quote: The next negative point of the game is, that it runs on Ethereum and unfortunately you have to deal with Ethereum Fees!

rebuttal.rebuttal: The absence of a password request or downline does not answer the actual allegation. The alleged mechanism is a paid node sold with recurring-return claims, and the video supplies both the required purchase amount and projected income. Showing a branded interface and leadership portraits establishes presentation, not that the advertised financial proposition is legitimate.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing-mechanism argument sets an unnecessarily narrow standard. A scam-like investment promotion need not request credentials or recruit a downline; the relevant question is whether viewers are encouraged to pay for promised returns. Here, the speaker says one node costs about $6,800, gives a projected annual figure, calls it a great investment, and links viewers to the description.
